title: A complete ultrametric on von Neumann's incomplete tensor products
abstract: We revisit von Neumann's theory of infinite tensor products of Hilbert spaces. On the set $Γ$ of equivalence classes of $C_0$-sequences, which labels the incomplete tensor products inside the complete tensor product, we introduce a natural pseudo-ultrametric $d$: the distance between two classes is the convergence exponent of the series $\sum_j|\langle\varphi_j,ψ_j\rangle-1|$ formed from any pair of representatives. We show that $d$ is well defined on equivalence classes, satisfies the strong triangle inequality, and is complete. Distinct classes may lie at distance zero, so $d$ separates points only after passing to the quotient $\widetildeΓ$ of $Γ$ by the relation $d=0$; the pair $(\widetildeΓ,d)$ is then a complete ultrametric space. As an application, we show that a product unitary $\bigotimes_j U$ whose factor $U$ satisfies $\inf_{\|x\|=1}|\langle x,Ux\rangle-1|>0$ (in particular, a unitary on a finite dimensional space with $1\notinσ(U)$) displaces every class to the maximal distance $1$. Guided by the intended application -- a caricature of Everettian branching, in which the sectors of the infinite tensor product play the role of worlds -- we also develop a gauge-invariant variant $\tilde d$ of the metric, based on von Neumann's weak equivalence and matched to the quasi-equivalence of product states on the quasi-local algebra. The displacement of a class under a product unitary, measured by $\tilde d$, is class dependent and realizes every value in $[0,1]$. We interpret $\tilde d$ as a decoherence exponent: it measures the polynomial rate at which two branches of the universal state vector become operationally distinct as ever larger portions of the environment are monitored.
summary: This paper develops a complete ultrametric structure on the space representing different 'worlds' or sectors arising from infinite tensor products. By defining metrics like the decoherence exponent ($	ilde{d}$), it provides a quantitative measure of how rapidly distinct branches become operationally distinguishable under unitary evolution. This offers a rigorous mathematical underpinning for interpreting quantum branching in the context of environmental monitoring.
main_problem: To mathematically formalize the concept of 'branching worlds' within quantum mechanics by defining a rigorous metric structure on von Neumann's incomplete tensor products.
main_result: The set of equivalence classes of these tensor product sectors forms a complete ultrametric space, providing a quantitative measure for state separation during unitary evolution.
method: The authors define two metrics ($d$ and $	ilde{d}$) based on convergence exponents derived from inner products between sequence representatives. They prove the properties of these metrics to establish the required mathematical structure.
model_or_system: The model is an infinite tensor product of Hilbert spaces, used as a mathematical framework for describing the Many-Worlds Interpretation (Everettian branching). The dynamics are governed by product unitaries acting on these sectors.
key_observables: The primary observables are the two metrics: $d$ (phase-sensitive) and $	ilde{d}$ (decoherence exponent), which quantify the rate of operational distinguishability between branches.
important_parameters: The convergence exponents ($p$) defining the metric, and the structure of the product unitaries $U(\otimes \varphi_i)$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a mathematical framework where sectors are labeled by equivalence classes ($\Gamma$), and it explicitly notes that it does not solve all conceptual difficulties of the Everett interpretation.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the pseudo-ultrametric $d$ on $\Gamma$, proving its completeness after quotienting by the zero-distance relation to form a true ultrametric space. It then develops the gauge-invariant metric $	ilde{d}$ and applies it to analyze how product unitaries cause displacement, interpreting this as decoherence.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous mathematical tool (ultrametrics) to quantify the emergence of apparent state reduction and environmental monitoring effects in quantum theory, which is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems dynamics.
